transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-07-22
Start time: 14:00 PT
Duration: 45 minutes (approx)
Redwood attendees: Jordan Kim (AE), Priya Shah (SE), Lee Carter (SE)
Customer attendees: Alicia Martinez (Head of AI), Tom Reynolds (CTO), Maya Patel (Data Engineer), Evan Liu (Clinical Ops)

Summary:
Quick scoping call to align on POC success criteria, workload sizing and the quality evaluation plan for HL7/clinical note summarization and triage use case. Discussed golden prompts, regression tests, hallucination checks, scoring, and timelines for a 1-week pilot followed by a larger 4-week evaluation.

Topics covered:
- Success criteria & KPIs (accuracy, hallucination rate, format compliance, latency/cost targets)
- Workload sizing (daily QPS, batch sizes, peak concurrency)
- Benchmark plan (datasets, golden prompts, regression suite, scoring approach)
- Infra/timeline (pilot schedule, dedicated vs hosted, telemetry to collect)
- Compliance notes (PHI handling, SOC2, KMS)

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Kim: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh quick intros, i'll run through agenda \u2014 we want to align on success criteria for the POC and agree on a quality eval plan, golden prompts etc, uh 45 minutes ish
[00:22] Alicia Martinez: hey Jordan, Alicia here, thanks, excited \u2014 our goal is to validate accuracy of clinical note summarization and ensure very low hallucinations for discharge instructions, so those are the two big ones
[00:38] Tom Reynolds: Tom \u2014 from infra side, curious about throughput, and how you recommend benchmarking for our on-prem traffic pattern, we run peaks around 300 requests per minute across our microservices
[00:54] Priya Shah: thanks \u2014 to set expectations, typical POC is 1-week pilot to validate quality with a small sample then a 4-week eval for throughput and edge cases. For the quality eval plan we suggest: golden prompt set, regression tests, hallucination/format checks, and a scoring approach that mixes automated metrics with human review
[01:18] Maya Patel: quick Q, what counts as "golden prompts" for you? are those hand-curated by us or you provide templates?
[01:30] Lee Carter: good question \u2014 usually it's collaborative: we provide prompt templates and example variants, customer supplies a set of canonical examples (the golden set) and we augment with paraphrases to test robustness
[01:46] Jordan Kim: for this use case we recommend ~100 golden prompts covering common note types (discharge summary, med reconciliation, triage notes), plus 300-500 additional samples for regression and scoring
[02:05] Evan Liu: are you okay with de-identified data only? we can't share PHI raw \u2014 will need guidance on redaction
[02:15] Priya Shah: absolutely, de-id only. we'll also provide a sample redaction checklist. For verification, synthetic augmentation is ok but we prefer real de-identified notes for fidelity
[02:31] Tom Reynolds: on the infra side, we may try both hosted API and a Dedicated reserved pool \u2014 what's your recommendation for latency vs cost tradeoffs?
[02:44] Priya Shah: if latency SLO is tight we recommend Dedicated with pinned capacity; for cost-speed tradeoff we can recommend quantized variants. For benchmarking we propose running the same models in hosted and dedicated configs to compare tail latency and token-cost
[03:03] Jordan Kim: let's talk success criteria \u2014 Alicia, what thresholds would you be satisfied with?
[03:12] Alicia Martinez: accuracy wise we need at least 92% extractive fidelity on key fields (meds, dosages, followup), hallucination rate below 2% on clinical facts, and format compliance for our EHR ingest (JSON schema) with <1% schema errors
[03:28] Priya Shah: great \u2014 we'll codify those as pass/fail and also produce continuous scoring. we'll capture metrics: exact match, F1 on entity extraction, hallucination count (facts not grounded), format-violation rate, and latency p95/p99
[03:48] Maya Patel: for scoring, do you run automatic checks first and then human review for edge cases?
[03:55] Lee Carter: yes, typical approach: automated scoring pipeline (F1, BLEU-ish for summaries, hallucination detectors) produces candidates flagged for human review. Then a small human panel (clinical SME) reviews flagged items and a random sample for spot checks
[04:15] Jordan Kim: on hallucination checks \u2014 we use a mix: rule-based checkers (e.g., impossible medication dosages), fact-check against patient record when available, and human adjudication. We'll also include format checks for JSON schema compliance and field-level validators
[04:36] Tom Reynolds: workload sizing \u2014 let me share numbers: regionally we expect 15k notes/day across batch jobs, but real-time API is about 300 rpm with bursts to 500 rpm during mornings
[04:50] Priya Shah: OK that's helpful \u2014 for the POC pilot we should pick a representative slice: 500-1,000 notes/day and a synthetic burst test to 600 rpm for a 30-minute window to stress tail latency
[05:06] Jordan Kim: benchmark plan overview:
- golden set: 100 canonical prompts (you provide 60, we add 40 paraphrases)
- regression set: 500 samples from de-id corpus
- hallucination bench: 200 targeted cases designed to probe hallucination-prone prompts
- format tests: 200 samples with edge-case formatting to validate JSON schema handling
[05:40] Maya Patel: who scores initial results? we have internal clinicians but limited time
[05:45] Priya Shah: we recommend a hybrid: Redwood runs automated scoring and flags; customer clinical SMEs review flagged cases and a 10% random sample. We can provide a simple scoring spreadsheet for adjudication to keep reviewer time low
[06:03] Alicia Martinez: timeline? when can we kick off the 1-week pilot?
[06:09] Jordan Kim: if we get samples this week (by 7/23) we can spin up the pilot environment and start tests 7/27. Pilot runs 7/27-7/31, then 4-week eval 8/3-8/28 if pilot passes gates
[06:26] Tom Reynolds: what are the gating criteria to move from pilot to full eval?
[06:31] Priya Shah: pilot gates: 1) automated metrics meet lower bound thresholds (e.g., >=90% key-field F1, hallucination <4%), 2) no major security blockers (SOC2 docs acceptable), 3) infra stability during burst tests (p95 < 800ms for real-time path)
[06:49] Jordan Kim: let's be specific about the scoring approach: scorecard will contain numeric metrics and pass/fail for each sample. We'll compute a weighted score: 50% entity F1, 20% hallucination penalty, 15% format compliance, 15% latency/cost normalized. Pass threshold 75% weighted score with hard cutoffs on hallucination and format errors
[07:18] Maya Patel: can you show an example scoring row?
[07:23] Lee Carter: yes, example: sample id, expected fields, predicted fields, F1=0.94, hallucinations=0, format_errors=0, latency_ms=320, weighted_score=82 -> pass. We will share scoring spreadsheet template after the call
[07:40] Alicia Martinez: about hallucination detection \u2014 how do you define an hallucination in structured outputs?
[07:47] Priya Shah: any factual assertion not present in the patient record or an invented medication/dose is an hallucination. For structured fields we'll do strict grounding checks; for free-text summaries we'll flag unsupported assertions and pass to human review
[08:03] Jordan Kim: on regression tests \u2014 we'll keep the suite as code in a repo, so each model iteration runs the same tests and we track regressions. We'll record baseline model outputs and diff on new runs
[08:18] Tom Reynolds: ok infra specifics \u2014 for the dedicated option what hardware do you propose?
[08:23] Priya Shah: for your throughput and latency targets we recommend a Dedicated pool of 4xA100-80GB (or equivalent Ampere gen) with batching tuned to keep p95 under 800ms for single-shot summarization. We'll provide cost estimates in the follow-up email
[08:42] Maya Patel: how will telemetry be surfaced? logs, token usage, error traces?
[08:47] Lee Carter: Redwood Console will give per-route latency histograms, token-level cost breakdown, sample-level outputs, and tracing hooks. We'll include a dashboard for the POC with the scoring metrics and flagged items
[09:04] Alicia Martinez: compliance: we need SOC2 plus KMS integration for keys \u2014 can you confirm?
[09:10] Jordan Kim: yes, Redwood supports SOC2, KMS/HSM for private deployments, and we can provide audit logs for the POC. We'll attach SOC2 and security pack in the follow-up
[09:22] Tom Reynolds: any blockers for data transfer? we prefer S3 bucket ingestion with temporary creds
[09:26] Priya Shah: S3 with temporary STS creds is standard \u2014 we can also support secure SharePoint if needed, but S3 is easiest for the test harness
[09:37] Jordan Kim: ok let's dig into the quality eval details a bit more \u2014 golden prompts, regression, hallucination checks and scoring approach
[09:45] Jordan Kim: golden prompts \u2014 definition: canonical input-output pairs that represent the "correct" output. For SummitCare we want 100 golden pairs across note types. We'll ask customer to provide 60 canonical and Redwood will author 40 paraphrases and edge-case variants
[10:04] Maya Patel: is 60 enough? some note types are rare
[10:08] Priya Shah: it's a pragmatic split \u2014 if you have more we can take 80/20, but 100 total gives statistical leverage for pass/fail during pilot. We will stratify by note type to ensure coverage of rare templates
[10:22] Lee Carter: regression tests \u2014 the suite will include: entity extraction checks, schema validation, hallucination probes, and end-to-end summary scoring. Regression suite stored as tests in a repo with CI to run against each model build
[10:36] Jordan Kim: hallucination/format checks \u2014 examples: medication invented (hallucination), contradictory dates, and missing allergy fields (format). We'll build rule-based detectors and a lightweight fact-checker that compares output fields to input source fields when possible
[10:50] Alicia Martinez: for scoring approach, you mentioned weighting \u2014 can that be tuned? we may want hallucination penalty higher
[10:57] Priya Shah: yes weights are configurable; for safety-critical clinical outputs customers tend to increase hallucination penalty to 30-40%. We'll provide a default and you can request a custom weighting before the pilot starts
[11:12] Tom Reynolds: about human review \u2014 what's the workload? how many samples per day would need clinician review?
[11:18] Jordan Kim: depends on your flag rate. For initial runs we expect auto flags to be around 8-12% of samples; if that is too high we can tune prompts and thresholds. For a 1k sample day that's about 80-120 reviews; we recommend a small clinical SME pool doing 20-30 reviews/day per SME for pilot
[11:40] Maya Patel: ok that's manageable for short pilot, but for broader rollout we'll need tooling to queue and triage reviews
[11:45] Lee Carter: Redwood Console has a review queue and adjudication UI; we can enable reviewer assignments and export adjudicated labels back to your system for model retraining
[12:00] Alicia Martinez: any recommended metrics dashboards?
[12:04] Priya Shah: yes we'll share a dashboard template showing weighted score over time, hallucination trend, schema violation rate, p95 latency, and cost per 1k notes. We'll also include a per-sample drilldown for failed items
[12:20] Jordan Kim: let's capture timeline and gating one more time:
- 7/23: customer shares de-id dataset and success criteria
- 7/24: Redwood sends eval template, scoring spreadsheet, and SOC2/security pack
- 7/27: pilot kickoff (7/27-7/31) running golden+regression suite and burst tests
- After pilot, review results and decide whether to proceed to 4-week eval (8/3-8/28)
[12:45] Tom Reynolds: what about benchmarks for tail latency under load? we want p99 < 2s ideally
[12:52] Priya Shah: we'll include p50/p95/p99 and recommend dedicated tuning for p99. p99 <2s is ambitious but achievable with dedicated pool and batch tuning; we'll show both token-cost and latency curves in the benchmark report
[13:10] Maya Patel: will you store outputs? we need retention options because of compliance
[13:15] Lee Carter: retention is configurable: for POC we can set short retention (7 days) and provide audit logs. For Private deployments you control retention via KMS and S3 lifecycle rules
[13:28] Alicia Martinez: ok good. Anything else on scoring approach?
[13:32] Jordan Kim: one more detail \u2014 for free-text summaries we'll use both overlap metrics (ROUGE/BLEU-ish) and a set of clinical fact checks (entity recall on key fields). The final weighted score blends these and applies penalties for hallucination and format errors
[13:50] Tom Reynolds: competition question \u2014 we evaluated Anthropic earlier; any differentiator you emphasize in POC?
[13:56] Priya Shah: we emphasize production-first telemetry, the rollout and fallback policies, and cost-aware controls (batching/quantization). For POC we'll show a cost/latency tradeoff chart across model variants
[14:12] Alicia Martinez: ok let's review next steps and owners
[14:16] Jordan Kim: recap: Jordan send eval template & SOC2 pack by 7/24; Priya share benchmark infra proposal by 7/26; Maya upload sample dataset by 7/23; schedule kickoff 7/27. Any objections?
[14:30] Maya Patel: none from me
[14:33] Tom Reynolds: fine
[14:34] Alicia Martinez: sounds good, thank you
[14:36] Jordan Kim: thanks everyone \u2014 we'll follow up with an email that contains the sample scoring spreadsheet, golden prompt templates, and the pilot checklist.

Appendix - Example scoring fields (to be included in template):
- sample_id (string)

- expected_entities (list)

- hallucination_count (number)
- format_errors (number)

- weighted_score (number)
- pass_fail (string)

References / shared artifacts mentioned:

- Security pack / SOC2 report (link in follow-up)

End of call.
